```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "C.UTF-8"))
library(data.table)
library(DT)
A <- "docs/assets/fdr"
ov <- fread(file.path(A, "fdr_overview.tsv"))
rounds <- fread(file.path(A, "adaptive_rounds.tsv"))
cal <- fread(file.path(A, "calibration.tsv"))
cons <- fread(file.path(A, "consistency.tsv"))
g <- fread(file.path(A, "significant_genes.tsv"))
fmt <- function(n) format(n, big.mark=",", trim=TRUE, scientific=FALSE)
pct <- function(x, digits=0) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f%%"), 100 * x)
interval <- function(lo, hi, digits=1) paste(pct(lo, digits), pct(hi, digits), sep=" - ")
any_tp <- ov[tp == "any timepoint"]
calp <- cal[tp == "all timepoints"]
cal_bh <- cal[measure == "runs with any BH discovery (q < 0.05)"]
fold <- function(gn, t) sprintf("%.1f", 2^g[gene == gn][[paste0("logFC_", t)]])
effect_reads <- function(d, t) fifelse(is.na(d[[paste0("dpsi_", t)]]), "no score",
  sprintf("%+.0f (%s)", 100 * d[[paste0("dpsi_", t)]], fmt(d[[paste0("het_cov_", t)]])))
best_q <- function(d) signif(pmin(d$q_bh_0hr, d$q_bh_1hr, d$q_bh_6hr, na.rm=TRUE), 2)
example_table <- function(genes, why) {
  d <- g[match(genes, gene)]
  data.table(Gene=d$gene, `0 hr`=effect_reads(d, "0hr"), `1 hr`=effect_reads(d, "1hr"), `6 hr`=effect_reads(d, "6hr"),
             `Best q`=best_q(d), `Het donors`=d$max_het, Relevance=why)
}
pattern_labels <- c("all three timepoints"="Significant at 3 timepoints",
                    "two timepoints"="Significant at 2 timepoints",
                    "shared, below threshold elsewhere"="One timepoint; nominal support elsewhere",
                    "candidate timepoint-specific"="One timepoint; no nominal support elsewhere",
                    "not testable elsewhere"="One timepoint; no usable score elsewhere")
g[, display_pattern := unname(pattern_labels[pattern])]
annot <- function(d) d[, .(`Neuronal GO term`=neuronal_go,
  `Developmental disorder or autism`=fifelse(nzchar(sfari) & nzchar(ddg2p), paste0(sfari, "; ", ddg2p), paste0(sfari, ddg2p)),
  `Expression after stimulation`=expression_response, `Splicing after stimulation`=fifelse(stim_splicing, "yes", ""))]
interactive_table <- function(d) DT::datatable(as.data.frame(d), rownames=FALSE, filter="top", extensions="Buttons",
  options=list(pageLength=10, lengthMenu=c(10, 25, 50, 150), scrollX=TRUE, order=list(), dom="Blfrtip", buttons=c("copy", "csv")),
  caption="Search or filter genes, sort columns, and export the filtered table as CSV.")
all3 <- g[pattern == "all three timepoints"]
sashimi_counts <- fread(file.path(A, "sashimi_summary.tsv"))
sashimi_donors <- fread(file.path(A, "sashimi_donor_counts.tsv"))
sashimi_normalized <- fread(file.path(A, "sashimi_normalized_counts.tsv"))
sashimi_calculation <- function(gn) {
  fraction <- function(i, e) sprintf("%d / (%d + %d) = %.1f%%", i, i, e, 100*i/(i+e))
  z <- rbindlist(lapply(c("0hr","1hr","6hr"),function(t){
    raw <- sashimi_counts[gene==gn & timepoint==t]
    norm <- sashimi_normalized[gene==gn & timepoint==t]
    stopifnot(nrow(raw)==1,nrow(norm)==1,
      round(norm$normalized_dPSI_unrounded,3)==raw$normalized_dPSI)
    data.table(Timepoint=sub("hr"," hr",t),Counts=c("Raw recorded","Normalized (test)"),
      `REF inclusion`=c(fraction(raw$REF_i,raw$REF_e),
                        fraction(norm$normalized_REF_i,norm$normalized_REF_e)),
      `ALT inclusion`=c(fraction(raw$ALT_i,raw$ALT_e),
                        fraction(norm$normalized_ALT_i,norm$normalized_ALT_e)),
      `ALT minus REF (pp)`=sprintf("%+.1f",100*c(raw$ALT_inclusion-raw$REF_inclusion,
                                               raw$normalized_dPSI)))
  }))
  knitr::kable(z,align="llllr")
}
sashimi_test_calculation <- function(gn) {
  d <- sashimi_donors[gene == gn & timepoint == "6hr" & usable %in% c("True", "TRUE", "true")]
  cols <- c("REF_e", "REF_i", "ALT_e", "ALT_i")
  n <- colSums(round(as.matrix(d[, ..cols]) * (mean(d$DP)/d$DP)))
  ref <- n["REF_i"] + n["REF_e"]; alt <- n["ALT_i"] + n["ALT_e"]
  effect <- sashimi_counts[gene == gn & timepoint == "6hr", normalized_dPSI]
  stopifnot(round(n["ALT_i"]/alt - n["REF_i"]/ref, 3) == effect)
  sprintf("At **6 hr**, the donor-normalized effect calculation is **100 x (%d/%d - %d/%d) = %+.1f percentage points** (ALT inclusion minus REF inclusion).",
    n["ALT_i"], alt, n["REF_i"], ref, 100*effect)
}
```

We extended the [chr9 permutation pilot](isolaser_permutation_pilot.html) to all
22 autosomes at baseline, 1 hour and 6 hours, using four donors. The aim is to
attach a permutation p-value and a **BH-adjusted p-value (q-value)** to each
allele–splicing association, with correction performed separately within each
timepoint.

**Main result:** `r fmt(any_tp$q05_associations)` associations in
**`r fmt(any_tp$q05_genes)` genes** have q < 0.05 and pass the original
`cis` / effect-size screen. `r nrow(all3)` genes meet these criteria at all
three timepoints. Calibration found no excess of false discoveries under the
chosen permutation null; its limits are described below.

# Genome-wide results

```{r overview}
counts <- function(a, b) sprintf("%s (%s)", fmt(a), fmt(b))
knitr::kable(ov[, .(Timepoint=tp, `Tested associations`=fmt(tested),
  `Paper's cutoff`=counts(paper_associations, paper_genes),
  Screen=counts(screen_associations, screen_genes),
  `Screen + q < 0.10`=counts(q10_associations, q10_genes),
  `Screen + q < 0.05`=counts(q05_associations, q05_genes))], align="lrrrrr")
```

Cells other than **Tested associations** show **associations (genes)**.

- **Paper's cutoff:** isoLASER's own `cis` call with no other filter, as in
  the isoLASER paper. It comes from isoLASER-joint, which pools every donor
  with ≥ 10 reads, homozygous donors included. It is counted over every
  association isoLASER reports, so it is not a subset of our tested
  associations. Above about 2,370 pooled reads, isoLASER's `cis` threshold
  falls below zero, so this column includes many calls with no effect.
- **Screen** (our definition), before FDR control: among our tested
  associations, isoLASER's `cis` rule recomputed on heterozygous donors only,
  plus |ΔPSI| ≥ 0.10. A tested association has at least one heterozygous donor
  (RNA allele fraction 0.25–0.75) with ≥ 30 informative reads, an exonic part
  ≥ 10 bp, and no other tested variant within 30 bp.

At q < 0.05,
`r pct(any_tp$q05_genes / any_tp$screen_genes)` of the screen's genes remain;
q < 0.10 adds `r fmt(any_tp$q10_genes - any_tp$q05_genes)` genes.
These counts use the recording rerun, so they can differ slightly from the
original [genome-wide screen](isolaser_genome_wide.html).

**Any timepoint** counts each gene or variant–part association once across
timepoints. BH targets FDR in each timepoint's full association family. The
effect-filtered subset shown here, its gene totals, and the union across
timepoints do not have a separate 5% FDR guarantee. Gene totals count genes
containing a qualifying association; they are not gene-level adjusted tests.

# How the test works

An **association** is a gene × variant × exonic part at one timepoint. An
exonic part is an interval defined by transcript exon boundaries and need not
be a complete exon. Reads form a 2 × 2 table: reference/alternative allele ×
part included/excluded. We combine eligible donors' tables using isoLASER's
own normalization and adjusted mutual information (**AMI**) functions. Higher
AMI means stronger allele–splicing association; values near zero indicate
little evidence, and slightly negative values are possible.

The tested family requires at least one donor with **≥30 informative reads
and RNA alternative-allele fraction 0.25–0.75**, a part ≥10 bp, and no other
tested variant less than 30 bp away. The donor rule is our operational
heterozygous-donor filter. Eligible associations without a computable observed
score stay in the family with p = 1.

For each permutation, we shuffle haplotype labels among reads **within donor,
gene and phasing group**. If a label changes, the read's allele is flipped at
every linked variant in that group. Unlabelled reads have their alleles
shuffled per variant. Each read's inclusion status, total coverage and the
original eligible donor set stay fixed. Before shuffling, reconstruction and
rescoring checks must reproduce the recording rerun's tables.

We count a **hit** when the shuffled AMI is at least as high as the observed
AMI. An undefined shuffled score also counts as a hit, conservatively:

\[
p = \frac{1 + \text{hits}}{1 + \text{shuffles}}.
\]

Every association starts with 1,000 shuffles. Those with fewer than 20 hits
continue to 10,000, 100,000 and finally 1,000,000 in total. Checkpoints and the
hit threshold were fixed in advance; this stopping rule is conservative
provided the underlying fixed-length permutation tests are valid. BH is then
applied to all eligible associations within each timepoint, before selecting
the `cis` / effect-size examples.

```{r rounds}
knitr::kable(rounds[, .(Timepoint=tp, `Stopped at 1,000`=fmt(stopped_1e3),
  `Stopped at 10,000`=fmt(stopped_1e4), `Stopped at 100,000`=fmt(stopped_1e5),
  `Reached 1,000,000`=fmt(reached_1e6))], align="lrrrr")
```

**Stopped** means the association had at least 20 hits at that checkpoint,
or had no observed score and received p = 1. Zero hits after a million shuffles
gives p = 1/1,000,001, approximately 10⁻⁶. Every tested association at this
minimum p-value has q < 0.05 in the current results.

# Calibration: how often are null signals reported?

We created **20 independently shuffled pseudo-observed datasets per
timepoint** and repeated the complete adaptive test and BH correction on
each. Donor eligibility was chosen from the original data and held fixed.
These 60 analyses are designed to remove the allele–splicing link: a discovery
in them is a false positive under this null. BH can occasionally report one
even when all associations are null, so we assess the frequency across runs.

```{r calibration_discoveries}
knitr::kable(cal_bh[, .(Timepoint=fifelse(tp == "all timepoints", "Pooled across timepoints", tp),
  `Null datasets`=runs, `Datasets with a BH discovery`=sprintf("%d/%d", runs_with_discovery, runs),
  `95% interval for that rate`=interval(lower_95, upper_95))], align="lrrr")
```

No dataset produced a BH discovery at q < 0.05; BY also produced none. The
intervals are binomial confidence intervals for the chance of **any**
discovery in an all-null analysis. Zero of 20 runs still allows a rate up to
**`r pct(cal_bh[tp == "0hr", upper_95], 1)` per timepoint**; pooling 60 datasets
gives an upper bound of `r pct(cal_bh[tp == "all timepoints", upper_95], 1)`
for the average rate. Pooling does not establish control separately at each
timepoint.

```{r calibration_pvalues}
cp <- calp[grepl("^share of p", measure)]
knitr::kable(cp[, .(Measure=measure, `Mean observed share`=pct(estimate, 3),
  `Approximate 95% interval`=interval(lower_95, upper_95, 3),
  `Nominal upper rate`=pct(nominal, 1))], align="lrrr")
```

These are mean shares across the 60 datasets, with approximate intervals from
the variation between runs. For example, p < 0.01 occurred for about
`r pct(cp[measure == "share of p < 0.01", estimate], 2)` of associations,
below the nominal 1%. Ties help explain this conservative behavior: when the
observed and shuffled AMIs are both zero, a tie counts as a hit. AMI is rounded
to three decimals by isoLASER.

**Interpretation:** calibration supports conservative behavior under our
permutation null. It does not prove validity for every association or estimate
the false-discovery proportion among the real-data results.

![](assets/fdr/qq.png)

The QQ plot compares p-values with a uniform reference. Real data (blue) have
more small p-values; calibration (grey) lies on or below the diagonal. The
upper plateau reflects the minimum attainable p-value.

# Genes to follow up

Here, **reported** means q < 0.05 plus the `cis` / effect-size screen. A gene
can contain several associations, and different associations can qualify at
different timepoints.

```{r patterns}
pat <- g[, .N, by=pattern][match(names(pattern_labels), pattern)][!is.na(pattern)]
knitr::kable(pat[, .(Pattern=unname(pattern_labels[pattern]), Genes=N)], align="lr")
```

For genes reported at only one timepoint, the last three categories describe
the representative association at the other timepoints: nominal p < 0.05,
p ≥ 0.05 where scored, or no usable score. They are descriptive categories,
not tests of an allele × time interaction. Among comparisons of significant
associations with another timepoint, `r pct(cons$nominal_p_lt_0.05)` had nominal
p < 0.05 there and `r pct(cons$same_sign)` had the same effect direction.

## Neuronal examples reported at all three timepoints

For each gene, the table follows its strongest reported association.
**0 / 1 / 6 hr** show the allelic effect in percentage points, with pooled
informative coverage in brackets. The stored effect is reference minus
alternative **exclusion**, equivalently **alternative minus reference
inclusion**: +10 means 10 percentage points higher inclusion on the alternative
allele. **Best q** is the lowest timepoint-specific q-value for this association;
**Het donors** is its maximum contributing donor count across timepoints, out
of four. **No score** means that timepoint lacks a usable effect estimate.

```{r ex_all3}
knitr::kable(example_table(c("HNRNPK", "ATL1", "KANSL1", "APLP2"), c(
  "Au-Kline syndrome (DDG2P), SFARI syndromic; GTEx brain sQTL comparison on the genome-wide page",
  "Hereditary spastic paraplegia (DDG2P); neuron projection development (GO)",
  "Koolen-de Vries syndrome (DDG2P); SFARI score 1",
  "APP family member; neuron projection development (GO)")), align="lrrrrrl")
```

These examples have neuronal or disorder annotations, but none meets our
expression- or splicing-response flag described below. **HNRNPK** is a
consistent allele-specific association across timepoints: zero hits in a
million shuffles at 0 and 1 hour, and four hits at 6 hours.

![](assets/fdr/HNRNPK_null.png)

Grey bars show only the first 1,000 shuffled scores; the blue line is the
observed score. The displayed p-values use the full adaptive run.

## Candidates for a change after stimulation

AHI1 is reported at 1 and 6 hours; WDR45B and KPNA2 at 6 hours only. Their
representative associations are weaker at earlier timepoints, making them
candidates for a direct comparison of allelic effects over time.

```{r ex_stimulation}
knitr::kable(example_table(c("AHI1", "WDR45B", "KPNA2"), c(
  sprintf("Joubert syndrome (DDG2P), SFARI syndromic; expression up %s-fold at 6 hr; junction-screen hit", fold("AHI1", "6hr")),
  sprintf("Expression up %s-fold at 1 hr", fold("WDR45B", "1hr")),
  sprintf("Synapse (GO); expression up %s-fold at 6 hr, below the 2-fold annotation rule", fold("KPNA2", "6hr")))), align="lrrrrrl")
```

For **AHI1**, variant chr6:135465851:C>T is significant for six exonic parts.
The highlighted part has a small baseline effect (−5 percentage points,
p = 0.46; 484 informative reads), compared with −24 and −29 points at 1 and
6 hours (p approximately 3 × 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁶). Other parts already show nominal
baseline associations, and coverage increases at 6 hours. This is a follow-up
candidate, not evidence that the variant becomes active only after stimulation.

![](assets/fdr/AHI1_null.png)

### Read alignments at all three timepoints

The following **isoLASER sashimi plots** use its `nigiri_plot` renderer, with
the project's plotting fixes and a layout for comparing 0, 1 and 6 hours.
Reads are separated into REF and ALT using **isoLASER's recorded allele
assignments for the exact variant–part association**. Each timepoint pools
only donors meeting the same criterion as the test: at least 30 informative
reads and an ALT fraction between 0.25 and 0.75. Donor IDs appear above the
tracks; the contributing donors can change between timepoints.

**How to read these plots:** blue is REF, orange is ALT, and yellow marks the
tested exonic part. Coverage heights and numbers on the curves are **raw
alignment counts**, with every junction supported by at least one read shown
(`-M 1 --min-junction-ratio 0`). All six tracks within a gene share the same
coverage scale. The transcript diagrams show representative local structures,
not every isoform.

**The inclusion percentage is a different quantity from an arc count.** A
label such as **65/137 (47.4%)** means 65 of 137 REF reads were assigned to
transcripts containing the tested part. isoLASER determines this from the
read's transcript assignment (`ZT`); a partial read may not physically reach
that part. Each panel therefore also gives the number of reads that actually
overlap the displayed window. The reported dPSI uses donor-normalized counts,
so it need not equal the difference between the two raw pooled percentages.

The calculations below distinguish **raw recorded counts** from the
**normalized counts used for the joint test**, at every timepoint. Each
fraction shows included / (included + excluded); inclusion and exclusion
come from transcript assignments. **No single junction arc is the statistical
test.** isoLASER tests the allele × part-included/excluded 2×2 table, using AMI
as the permutation statistic. dPSI describes the effect size. Donor tables are
scaled to their mean depth and rounded before pooling. **Both AMI and dPSI
use the normalized 2×2 table**; the permutation p-value and BH q-value are
based on that analysis. These rescaled counts are not extra sequenced reads.
The sashimi coverage and arcs remain raw so they describe observed alignments.

For example, **WDR45B at 1 hour** has raw inclusion **42/150 = 28.0% REF**
and **77/206 = 37.4% ALT**, a raw difference of **+9.4 pp**. The normalized
test table instead has **42 included / 109 excluded for REF** and
**74 included / 133 excluded for ALT**. Its effect is
**100 × (74/207 − 42/151) = +7.9 pp**, matching the reported dPSI.
Both versions are now labelled in the figures and shown in the tables.

#### AHI1: alternative exon usage

The highlighted 85-base part is an annotated exon in some transcripts; other
transcripts skip it. Assigned inclusion is lower for ALT than REF, with a
larger difference at 1 and 6 hours. Read depth and the donor set also change,
so these panels do not establish an allele-by-stimulation interaction.

![](assets/fdr/AHI1_sashimi.png)

**Tested association:** chr6:135465851:C>T versus inclusion of the yellow
85-base part, chr6:135495813–135495898 (isoLASER's 0-based coordinates).
Arcs jumping over this part support exclusion; arcs joining it to neighboring
exons support inclusion. The other arcs provide transcript context.

```{r ahi1_sashimi_calculation}
sashimi_calculation("AHI1")
```

**Where does the 140 come from? AHI1, 6 hr, REF allele:**

```{r ahi1_ref_donor_breakdown}
ahi1_ref_breakdown <- sashimi_donors[gene == "AHI1" & timepoint == "6hr" &
  usable %in% c("True", "TRUE", "true"),
  .(Donor=donor, `Part included`=REF_i, `Part excluded`=REF_e)]
ahi1_ref_breakdown <- rbind(ahi1_ref_breakdown, data.table(
  Donor="Total", `Part included`=sum(ahi1_ref_breakdown$`Part included`),
  `Part excluded`=sum(ahi1_ref_breakdown$`Part excluded`)))
knitr::kable(ahi1_ref_breakdown, align="lrr")
```

**Included: 46 + 39 + 55 = 140. Excluded: 59 + 47 + 48 = 154.**
Therefore, **140 / (140 + 154) = 47.6%**. Each read is counted once, using
whether its assigned transcript contains the yellow part; these are **not sums
of arc labels**. CD_21 is excluded at this timepoint because its ALT fraction
(0.759) exceeds the donor-filter maximum of 0.75.

`r sashimi_test_calculation("AHI1")`

[Open AHI1 as PDF](assets/fdr/AHI1_sashimi.pdf) to enlarge junction labels.

#### WDR45B: limited direct coverage of the alternative exon

This part belongs to an alternative exon near the transcript's 3-prime end.
**Treat this as a candidate requiring validation.** Many reads are assigned
an inclusion status from their transcript identity without reaching this
region: at 6 hours only **1 of 370 ALT reads** overlaps the displayed window.
The assigned ALT inclusion of 186/370 (50.3%) therefore has very little direct
local alignment support in this plot. WDR45B is a weaker visualization example
than its association statistics alone suggest.

![](assets/fdr/WDR45B_sashimi.png)

**Tested association:** chr17:82643963:C>T versus inclusion of the yellow
220-base part, chr17:82626788–82627008 (0-based). The long arc crossing the
yellow band supports its exclusion; the test counts assigned inclusion as
well as exclusion, including partial reads that do not reach this window.

```{r wdr45b_sashimi_calculation}
sashimi_calculation("WDR45B")
```

`r sashimi_test_calculation("WDR45B")`

[Open WDR45B as PDF](assets/fdr/WDR45B_sashimi.pdf).

#### KPNA2: a retained intron segment

The yellow 100-base part is removed as an intron in some transcripts and
retained within a longer exon in others. An arc across the yellow interval
supports **removal** of the part; continuous aligned coverage through it
supports retention. Assigned inclusion is higher for ALT, with the largest
normalized difference at 6 hours (+11.6 percentage points). Partial reads and
transcript assignments still explain why the inclusion totals are not simply
the sum of local junction counts.

![](assets/fdr/KPNA2_sashimi.png)

**Tested association:** chr17:68035783:T>C versus retention of the yellow
100-base part, chr17:68042999–68043099 (0-based). The short arc exactly across
this band supports **removal**, not retention: at 6 hr it has **187 REF and
135 ALT reads**. Those arc counts are not the full excluded-read totals,
because isoLASER uses transcript assignments for all informative reads.

```{r kpna2_sashimi_calculation}
sashimi_calculation("KPNA2")
```

`r sashimi_test_calculation("KPNA2")`

[Open KPNA2 as PDF](assets/fdr/KPNA2_sashimi.pdf).

are reported at 1 hour with nominal support at another timepoint.

## Full interactive gene table

The table includes all **`r nrow(g)` reported genes**. The variant, part,
timepoint effects, best q and donor count refer to the representative
association; **Significant at** describes the gene across all its associations.

```{r all}
interactive_table(cbind(g[, .(Gene=gene, Pattern=display_pattern, `Significant at`=sig_tps,
  `0 hr`=effect_reads(g, "0hr"), `1 hr`=effect_reads(g, "1hr"), `6 hr`=effect_reads(g, "6hr"),
  `Best q`=best_q(g), `Het donors`=max_het)], annot(g),
  g[, .(Variant=variant_qual, `Exonic part`=exonic_part)]))
```

The four annotations below help select examples; they are exploratory and are
not enrichment tests or evidence of stimulation-dependent allelic effects.

| Annotation | Rule |
|:--|:--|
| Neuronal GO term | Curated, non-electronic GO annotation to synapse, neuron projection, synaptic signaling, neuron projection development or neuron death. |
| Developmental disorder or autism | SFARI score 1, 2 or syndromic; or a strong/definitive DDG2P association. Not all listed disorders are neurological. |
| Expression after stimulation | In the 100-line cohort of [Liang et al., Science 2026](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adw3949), pooled expression changes ≥2-fold at 1 or 6 hours with the same direction in ≥75% of lines. This is a descriptive check, without a statistical test. |
| Splicing after stimulation | A junction-usage hit in our [long-read stimulation screen](splicing_candidates.html). |

<!-- # Interpretation limits -->

<!-- - This is within-donor allele-specific splicing analysis with four donors; -->
<!--   `r g[max_het == 1, .N]` of the `r nrow(g)` reported genes have a representative -->
<!--   association supported by one heterozygous donor. It does not establish a -->
<!--   population-level sQTL. -->
<!-- - Significance at one timepoint and not another does not demonstrate a change -->
<!--   with stimulation. That requires a direct allele × time test. -->
<!-- - Permutation does not eliminate alignment or variant-calling artifacts. -->
<!--   HLA-A and HLA-C warrant particular mapping checks because of their polymorphism. -->
<!-- - Rounded scores and conservative treatment of undefined shuffles can reduce -->
<!--   power. Failure to pass the screen does not establish absence of an effect. -->
